lessonTitle: Peripheral Nerve Injury Cases and Dermatomes

blocks.text: A man sleeps for hours with his arm hanging over the back of a chair and wakes with a wrist that will not extend and a hand that hangs limp. His grip is hopeless because he cannot cock the wrist. The pattern of what is lost points to one nerve, and the place where that nerve is exposed explains why it was injured.

blocks.markdown: Peripheral nerve cases are solved in three steps. First, ask which muscles are weak (the **motor deficit**). Second, ask where sensation is lost (the **sensory deficit**). Third, ask where along its course the nerve is superficial, tethered or compressed (the **site of vulnerability**). A deficit that fits one nerve's motor and sensory territory points to that nerve; a deficit that follows a band across the limb points to a spinal root.

blocks.title: Dermatome
blocks.text: The area of skin supplied by the sensory fibres of a single spinal nerve root. Adjacent dermatomes overlap, so loss of one root often produces only a small area of true numbness, whereas a peripheral nerve has a more sharply defined territory.

rows: Carpal tunnel at the wrist; supracondylar fracture of the humerus
At the wrist: weak thumb abduction and opposition, thenar wasting; higher: also weak flexion of index and middle fingers
Palmar surface of lateral three and a half digits
Behind the medial epicondyle at the elbow; hook of hamate at the wrist
Weak finger abduction and adduction, claw posture of ring and little fingers, positive Froment sign
Little finger and medial half of the ring finger
Spiral groove of the humerus (midshaft fracture, compression)
Wrist drop, weak finger and thumb extension
Dorsum of the lateral hand, especially the first dorsal web space
Foot drop: weak dorsiflexion and eversion
Lateral leg and dorsum of the foot
blocks.caption: Deficits after injury to four commonly tested nerves.

blocks.title: Localising a median nerve lesion
blocks.prompt: A woman has night-time tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers, thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction, but flexion of her index and middle finger tips is normal. Where is the lesion?

steps.text: Sensory loss in the lateral three and a half digits on the palm points to the median nerve.
Thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction indicate involvement of the muscles supplied by its recurrent branch.
Normal finger flexion means the branches given off in the forearm are intact, so the lesion is distal to them.
The most likely site is the carpal tunnel, under the flexor retinaculum, where the nerve is compressed.

blocks.answer: Median nerve compression at the carpal tunnel.

blocks.markdown: **Why each nerve is vulnerable.** The median nerve lies beneath the flexor retinaculum in a tight tunnel, so swelling compresses it; it is also at risk in supracondylar fractures of the humerus. The ulnar nerve passes in a groove behind the medial epicondyle and lies just under the skin, so a blow there (the funny bone) or chronic leaning can injure it. The radial nerve winds round the humerus in the spiral groove, in contact with bone, so midshaft fractures or prolonged compression damage it; its high branches to triceps leave before the groove, so triceps is usually spared. The common peroneal nerve winds around the neck of the fibula just under the skin with no muscle padding, so fractures, tight casts or crossed legs can injure it.

blocks.title: Peroneal nerve or L5 root?
blocks.prompt: A patient has foot drop with loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot. Weakness is limited to dorsiflexion and eversion, and inversion of the foot is normal. Which diagnosis fits better: a common peroneal nerve lesion or an L5 root lesion?

steps.text: The common peroneal nerve supplies dorsiflexors and evertors but not the inverters (tibialis posterior is supplied by the tibial nerve).
An L5 root lesion would be expected to weaken inversion and hip abduction as well, because those muscles also receive L5 fibres.
Inversion is normal, so the deficit is confined to the peroneal territory.
The common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck is more likely.

blocks.answer: Common peroneal nerve lesion at the fibular neck.

rows: Lateral upper arm over the deltoid
Dorsum of the foot and great toe
blocks.caption: Key dermatome landmarks.

blocks.markdown: A root lesion typically produces sensory loss in a dermatomal band, pain radiating along it, weakness in the muscles sharing that root (the myotome), and sometimes a depressed reflex, for example the ankle reflex in S1. Because dermatomes overlap and nerve fibres are redistributed in the plexuses, the pattern of a root lesion differs from that of a single peripheral nerve.

items: Test power in the key muscles and note which are weak.
Map sensory loss and compare with nerve territories and dermatomes.
Ask where the nerve is superficial or compressed at the site of the injury.
Decide whether the pattern fits one nerve, one root or both.

blocks.title: Think nerve, then site
blocks.text: Name the nerve from the deficit, then name the place on its course where it is vulnerable. The injury mechanism and the anatomy usually fit together.

blocks.title: Radial wrist drop is not weak triceps
blocks.text: In spiral groove injury the branches to triceps have already left the nerve, so elbow extension is preserved and the problem is extension at the wrist and fingers.

points: Median: thenar weakness and lateral palmar sensory loss, vulnerable at the carpal tunnel and in supracondylar fracture.
Ulnar: claw hand, weak finger abduction and adduction, little finger sensory loss, vulnerable behind the medial epicondyle.
Radial: wrist drop, vulnerable in the spiral groove. Common peroneal: foot drop, vulnerable at the neck of the fibula.
Dermatomes are bands supplied by one root; examples are C6 thumb, T10 umbilicus and L5 dorsum of the foot.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old rugby player fractures the midshaft of his humerus. Afterwards he cannot extend his wrist but can still extend his elbow. Which nerve is injured and where?

options.text: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
Median nerve at the wrist
Ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle
Axillary nerve at the surgical neck

questions.correctOptionText: Radial nerve in the spiral groove

distractorRationale.a: Correct: wrist drop with preserved triceps points to a radial lesion in the spiral groove.
distractorRationale.b: Median injury would impair thumb opposition and finger flexion, not wrist extension.
distractorRationale.c: Ulnar injury affects the intrinsic muscles of the hand.
distractorRationale.d: Axillary injury affects deltoid and sensation over the shoulder.

questions.explanation: The radial nerve contacts the humerus in the spiral groove, and branches to triceps leave before this point. Midshaft fracture therefore causes wrist drop with preserved elbow extension.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man who sat for hours with his legs crossed now has foot drop and loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot and the lateral leg. Which nerve and site are most likely involved?

options.text: Common peroneal nerve at the neck of the fibula
Tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa
Femoral nerve at the inguinal ligament
Sciatic nerve in the gluteal region

questions.correctOptionText: Common peroneal nerve at the neck of the fibula

distractorRationale.a: Correct: common peroneal compression at the fibular neck causes foot drop.
distractorRationale.b: Tibial injury weakens plantarflexion and inversion.
distractorRationale.c: Femoral nerve injury weakens knee extension.
distractorRationale.d: Sciatic injury would affect both divisions, including plantarflexion.

questions.explanation: The common peroneal nerve is superficial and unprotected at the fibular neck. Compression there causes loss of dorsiflexion and eversion and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.

questions.stem: After a fall onto the elbow, a patient has a claw posture of the ring and little fingers, cannot adduct the fingers and has numbness of the little finger. Which nerve is injured?

options.text: Ulnar nerve
Radial nerve
Median nerve
Axillary nerve

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the ulnar pattern.
distractorRationale.b: Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop.
distractorRationale.c: Median nerve injury affects thumb and lateral fingers.
distractorRationale.d: Axillary nerve injury affects the shoulder.

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies most intrinsic hand muscles, including interossei, and the skin of the little finger. It runs behind the medial epicondyle, which makes it vulnerable at the elbow.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the common peroneal nerve is vulnerable at the knee?

options.text: It winds around the neck of the fibula directly beneath the skin
It passes through the carpal tunnel
It runs in the spiral groove
It lies in the cubital tunnel

questions.correctOptionText: It winds around the neck of the fibula directly beneath the skin

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it is superficial where it winds around the fibular neck.
distractorRationale.b: The carpal tunnel contains the median nerve.
distractorRationale.c: The spiral groove is on the humerus and contains the radial nerve.
distractorRationale.d: The cubital tunnel contains the ulnar nerve.

questions.explanation: The nerve has little soft tissue padding at the fibular neck, so pressure or fracture there injures it.

questions.stem: A woman has a numb thumb, weakness of the biceps and diminished sensation over the lateral forearm after a neck injury. Which dermatome is mainly involved?

options.text: C6
C8
T4
L5

distractorRationale.a: Correct: C6 corresponds to the thumb.
distractorRationale.c: T4 corresponds to the nipple line.
distractorRationale.d: L5 is the dorsum of the foot.

questions.explanation: The thumb dermatome is C6. Radiating lateral forearm and thumb symptoms suggest a C6 root lesion.

questions.stem: A band-like area of numbness extending from the umbilicus laterally around the trunk is typical of a T10 root lesion.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: T10 supplies the skin at the level of the umbilicus. Root lesions produce bands that follow the dermatomes, unlike peripheral nerves that have sharply defined territories.

questions.stem: Compared with a lesion of a peripheral nerve, a single spinal root lesion typically produces:

options.text: Sensory loss over a dermatomal band with overlap from neighbouring roots
Sensory loss limited to the exact territory of a named nerve
Complete anaesthesia of the whole limb
No motor deficit ever

questions.correctOptionText: Sensory loss over a dermatomal band with overlap from neighbouring roots

distractorRationale.a: Correct: root lesions follow dermatomes, which overlap.
distractorRationale.c: A single root does not abolish sensation of a whole limb.
distractorRationale.d: Roots supply myotomes, so weakness may occur.

questions.explanation: Dermatomes overlap so numbness from one root may be limited, and the pattern is a band rather than the territory of one nerve.

questions.stem: A patient has weak thumb abduction, thenar wasting and loss of sensation over the palm of the lateral three and a half digits. Name the nerve, the likely site of injury and why it is vulnerable there.
markingGuide: Carpal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum.
Nerve lies in a tight space with the flexor tendons.
Alternative site: supracondylar fracture if forearm flexors also weak.
questions.explanation: The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel under the flexor retinaculum with nine tendons, so any increase in pressure compresses it. Sensory loss in the lateral palm and thenar weakness fit the median territory.

questions.stem: Compare the features of an L5 root lesion with a common peroneal nerve lesion in a patient with foot drop.
markingGuide: Both cause weak dorsiflexion and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.
L5 lesion also weakens inversion (tibialis posterior) and hip abduction.
Common peroneal lesion spares inversion and hip abduction.
L5 lesion may cause back pain radiating down the leg.
Common peroneal lesion often follows trauma or compression at the fibular neck.
questions.explanation: The key discriminator is the muscles that fall outside the peroneal territory yet receive L5 fibres. Inversion and hip abduction are weak in an L5 lesion but preserved in a common peroneal lesion.

questions.stem: Describe how dermatomal sensory loss can be used to localise a spinal root lesion, and why neighbouring roots may hide a small lesion.
markingGuide: Dermatomes are skin areas supplied by one root.
Map the area of sensory loss and match to dermatome landmarks (for example C6 thumb, T10 umbilicus).
Check myotomes and reflexes for the same root.
Overlap of adjacent dermatomes means one root lesion causes a small area of true loss.
Band pattern distinguishes it from a peripheral nerve.
questions.explanation: Each root has a characteristic band, so mapping the area of loss indicates the segment. Overlap from neighbouring roots reduces the area of complete loss and may hide a single lesion.
